concept.name: Federal funds rate
concept.definition: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight, uncollateralized. The FOMC sets a target rate or range for it, and the New York Fed publishes the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) as the volume-weighted median of actual transactions.
concept.intuition: It is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of their reserve balances at the Fed — the rate U.S. monetary policy directly targets.
concept.mechanics: The federal funds market consists of domestic unsecured overnight borrowings in U.S. dollars by depository institutions from other institutions, primarily GSEs. The EFFR is computed as a volume-weighted median of transactions reported on the FR 2420 report and published for the prior business day at about 9:00 a.m.; the Desk's operations keep it within the FOMC's target range.
concept.failure_modes: The fed funds market is thin and dominated by specific players (GSEs lending to banks), so the EFFR can be unrepresentative of marginal funding costs; the rate also lost its role as the sole steering variable once abundant reserves made administered rates the main control tools.
concept.misconceptions: The Fed does not directly set the market fed funds rate by decree — it sets a target range and uses operations and administered rates to steer the traded rate into it.
concept.example: With an FOMC target range of 3.50–3.75%, the EFFR typically prints near the middle of the range, e.g. 3.62%.
